Rare 1969 Dodge Charger Daytona Has Been in the Same Family Since New, True Hemi Gem
19 photos
Photo: Mecum Auctions
Introduced in 1966, the Dodge Charger hit NASCAR ovals as soon as it arrived in showrooms. It won the title that very first year, but it struggled during the following season. With the regular Charger unable to keep up with the Ford Torino Talladega , Dodge developed more aerodynamic versions.
In 1969, Dodge created the Charger 500. Compared to the R/T, it featured a 1968 Coronet grille, while the rear window was made flush with the rest of the roof. These changes reduced both drag and lift. However, the 500 still wasn't quick enough for the Torino Talladega on the high-bank oval tracks.
Later that year, Dodge took things up a notch and developed the Daytona. Far more radical than the Charger 500, the Daytona was a whopping 18 inches (457 mm) longer thanks to a nose cone, while massive wing sat 23 inches (547 mm) atop the trunk.
To make the Daytona eligible for NASCAR racing, Dodge was required to sell at least 500 cars to the general public. Mopar eventually put together 503 examples, which sold like hotcakes. At the time of its introduction, the Daytona was by far the most radical production vehicle available in the United States.
The Charger Daytona came standard with the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB V8, which was also the base mill in the R/T. The unit delivered 375 horsepower and 480 pound-feet (651 Nm) of torque. The 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi, rated at 425 horsepower and 490 pound-feet (664 Nm), was on the options list.
Most Daytonas rolled off the assembly line with the standard engine. Specifically, 433 units got the 440 V8. The figure is split between 139 cars equipped with the four-speed manual and 294 fitted with the three-speed TorqueFlite automatic.
The remaining 70 units were ordered with the 426 Hemi. Exactly 22 customers went with the four-speed manual, while 48 opted for the comfort of the automatic gearbox. The B5 Blue example you see here is one of those Hemi automatic rigs, and it's quite stunning.
Ordered new at Walt Sparrow Dodge in Greeley, Colorado, this Daytona soldiered on for over 50 years with its 426-cubic-inch Hemi V8 still intact. What's more, it's a highly original example with just one repaint in the original color.
In the care of the same family since new, the Mopar has only 43,041 miles on the odometer and an overall condition that makes it suitable as a museum display. It also has the desirable A32 Super Performance Axle Package, which pairs the drivetrain with a Dana 60 Sure Grip rear end with a 4.10 ratio.
This Charger Daytona recently popped up among the lots that will go under the hammer at Mecum's Kissimmee 2027 auction . It will change hands on January 15, and there's no way that it will fetch less than $700,000. Assuming that bidding will blow past the reserve, this Daytona may become one of the most expensive units ever sold at public auction.
For reference, the most expensive Hemi Daytona sold for $3.3 million in 2024. Two more cars traded for seven-figure sums. One sold for $1.43 million in 2023, while another winger warrior fetched $1.32 million in 2026.
